title: Apply basic entrepreneurial principles to farming

lessons.title: The farm as a business
lessons.html:
The farm as a business

A farm is a business. It must make a profit to survive, pay workers, repay loans and invest in the future. An entrepreneurial farmer or supervisor looks for opportunities, manages risk, controls costs and keeps improving. This applies whether you run a 2-hectare vegetable plot or supervise a section of a large commercial farm.

Entrepreneurial principles in farming

  • Market first: produce what buyers want, in the quantity, quality and timing they need. Find the buyer before you plant.
  • Add value: grading, packing, processing (for example making jam, drying fruit or selling slaughtered and packed chickens instead of live birds) can increase income.
  • Control costs: know what each input costs and use it efficiently.
  • Manage risk: spread risk over more than one product or market, insure where possible, and keep a cash reserve.
  • Innovate: try better cultivars, water-saving irrigation or new markets, but test on a small scale first.
  • Build networks: co-operatives, study groups, input suppliers, extension officers and buyers.

Understanding the market

Ask: who are my customers (fresh produce market, retailer, spaza shops, schools, processors, exporters)? What price will they pay? What standards do they require? When do they buy? Who are my competitors? How will I deliver?

Fresh produce prices at markets such as the Johannesburg and Tshwane fresh produce markets change daily with supply and demand. Planting when everyone else plants often means selling when prices are lowest. Planning to harvest slightly earlier or later can earn better prices.

Contracts

Some buyers, such as processors and retailers, offer contracts with an agreed price and quantity. Contracts reduce price risk but you must meet the volume and quality standards. Read and understand a contract before signing.

lessons.title: Costs, profit and the enterprise budget
lessons.html:
Costs, profit and the enterprise budget

Types of costs

  • Variable (direct) costs: change with the size of production. Seed, fertiliser, feed, chemicals, fuel, packaging, casual labour, transport.
  • Fixed (overhead) costs: stay the same whatever you produce. Permanent wages, insurance, loan interest, depreciation of machinery, rates.

The enterprise budget

An enterprise budget shows the expected income and costs for one enterprise, such as one hectare of cabbages or a batch of broilers.

Item (1 ha cabbage)Amount (R)
Income: 30 000 heads x R6180 000
Seedlings18 000
Fertiliser and lime22 000
Crop protection15 000
Irrigation electricity9 000
Labour30 000
Transport and market commission26 000
Total variable costs120 000
Gross margin60 000

These figures are an example only; use your own prices.

Gross margin = income minus variable costs. Fixed costs must still be paid out of the gross margins of all enterprises. Net profit = total gross margin minus fixed costs.

Break-even

Break-even price = total cost / number of units. If cabbages cost R120 000 to produce for 30 000 heads, the break-even is R4 per head before fixed costs. Below that price you lose money.

Cash flow

Costs come months before income. A cash flow plan shows money in and out each month, so you know when you will need finance. Many profitable farms fail because they run out of cash.

Records and finance

Keep records of all income and expenses, separate from personal money. Banks, the Land Bank and development finance institutions will want a business plan, budgets and records before lending.

Key points

  • Treat the farm as a business: market first, add value, control costs, manage risk.
  • Know your buyers, their standards and price patterns before planting.
  • Variable costs change with production; fixed costs do not.
  • Gross margin = income minus variable costs; net profit = gross margins minus fixed costs.
  • Plan cash flow and keep good records to get finance and survive.
